title: Tracing Cache Inconsistencies to Their Root Cause
body_markdown:
*How Nextdoor added verification keys to its Valkey cache so every inconsistency with Postgres comes with a root cause, and the bugs they uncovered*


Keeping a cache consistent is only half the problem. In our previous series, versioned writes kept our Valkey cache from going backwards, and a reconciler deleted stale entries left behind by missed or racing writes. What that series didn’t answer is the question that comes right after every fix: what broke in the first place? A self-healing cache repairs the symptom and erases the evidence. This post is about how we taught our cache to keep receipts, so that every inconsistency comes with a cause, and how those receipts led us to bugs that lived outside our caching logic.


### Background: how the cache stays consistent


In our[Scaling Nextdoor’s Datastores](https://engblog.nextdoor.com/scaling-nextdoors-datastores-part-1-234d0cf67665) series,[Part 4](https://engblog.nextdoor.com/scaling-nextdoors-datastores-part-4-c9d3d3edcd34) covered versioned rows and conditional cache writes, and[Part 5](https://engblog.nextdoor.com/scaling-nextdoors-datastores-part-5-5221da60f374) covered the reconciler, which consumes Postgres’s change stream to find and delete stale cache entries left behind by missed or racing writes. A quick recap:


Nextdoor serves a large share of its Postgres reads from an ORM cache in Valkey. Each cached row carries its db_version, a monotonically increasing counter that a Postgres trigger bumps on every update. Writers never blindly overwrite the cache: they call set_if_version, a Valkey Lua function that replaces the cached value only if the incoming version is newer.


The conditional set keeps the cache from going backwards, but the cache can still end up out of date in a few ways: a write can commit to Postgres and never reach Valkey, two requests can race, or a slow request can fill the cache from a read that is already stale.


To catch these, our **reconciler** consumes Postgres’s change stream (change data capture, or CDC) and checks each change against the cache twice:


- **Pass 1** , immediately: del_if_version compares versions and deletes the cached entry if it’s older than the change.
- **Pass 2** , a few seconds later: the same check. Pass 1 often beats the application’s own cache write, so a stale entry there is usually a race about to resolve. A stale entry at **pass 2** means something went wrong.


### The problem: the reconciler saw what, never why


The reconciler fixed inconsistencies, but every pass 2 alert raised the same question: was it an application bug (a code path that updates Postgres but not the cache), an infrastructure failure (a Valkey write that timed out), or a harmless race? To the reconciler, all three look identical. Answering meant digging through logs, usually without success.


As we cached more data models, each with its own write paths, this got worse. We needed to tell real bugs from expected races, and to trust our inconsistency metrics. An alert reading “N inconsistencies on pass 2” gives on-call nothing to act on. “Model X is being filled from a stale read” does.


### Design: every cache write leaves a receipt


In[Part 4](https://engblog.nextdoor.com/scaling-nextdoors-datastores-part-4-c9d3d3edcd34) , we shared the interface for set_if_version. We extended it so that, alongside the cached value, it also writes a second, small key: a verification key, or receipt, recording who wrote that version and why. Here’s the updated interface:


```text
--- Sets a key only if the supplied version is newer than the stored version,  --- and writes a receipt for that version in the same atomic call.  -- @param context (string) Who wrote this version: service, trace ID, and the version it replaced.  -- @param operation (string) "fill_on_write" or "fill_on_miss".  -- @param skip_verification_key (boolean) Skip the receipt for keys the reconciler never checks.  function set_if_version(key, version, metadata, value, ttl, context, operation, skip_verification_key) ... end   -- each receipt is stored under:  verification:{<cache key>}:<db_version>
```


A Lua function in Valkey Cluster can only touch keys in one hash slot. The {…} hash tag puts the receipt in the same slot as its cache key, so both are written atomically: if the cache write happened, so did the receipt.


Each receipt records:


- the **operation** : fill_on_write (after a database commit) or fill_on_miss (after a cache miss);
- the **service** and **trace ID** of the writer;
- the **version that was in the cache** at write time.


***Author’s Note:*** *The operation tells you what kind of write it was, but not where it came from. We added the service and trace ID so any receipt can be followed back to the exact request that wrote it, and that context is how we tracked down the bugs below.*


On the read side, del_if_version returns two receipts along with the comparison result: one for the version being checked and one for the version currently cached.


```text
-- {comparison, delete_result, receipt_for_checked_version, receipt_for_cached_version}  return {"gt", "ok", verification_key_value, stored_verification_key_value}
```


With both, the reconciler can tell “the app wrote v8, but a stale v7 fill landed after it” from “the app never wrote v8.”


### Reading the receipts


del_if_version returns one of four comparison results:


Pass 2 carries most of the signal. For eq and lt, look at the receipt for the version being checked; for gt, look at the receipt on the stale value in the cache.


The lt / none row is the one we couldn’t see before: a later write hides the bug from the cache, but not from the receipts.


The reconciler emits a single metric per reconciled change, tagged with the model and both passes’ comparison results and receipts, so every inconsistency is classified by model on one dashboard.


### Keeping receipts cheap


One receipt per cache write adds up, so receipts live only as long as they’re useful. The reconciler expires each one after pass 2 reads it. Read fills never trigger a reconciler visit, so their receipts expire on their own after a few minutes. And where the reconciler never looks, we skip receipts entirely: cached attribute lookups, and a row’s first version, which comes from an insert the reconciler doesn’t check.


### What it found


The new metric surfaced three bugs, none of them in our caching logic.


**A silent failure in the reconciler.** For one of our busiest data models, many changes had no pass-1 data at all. A context-cancellation bug let pass 1 fail quietly while pass 2 went ahead.


**Deleted rows coming back.** Pass 2 alerts on one of our tables showed gt with the writer’s fill_on_write receipt present, but *no* receipt on the stale cached value. Since only first versions skip receipts, that pointed at a row that had been re-inserted. The cause was an update racing a delete: when the ORM’s save() matched zero rows, it fell back to an INSERT and recreated the deleted row at version 1. Forcing an UPDATE fixed it.


**Duplicate background jobs.** A later alert on the same table showed gt with a fill_on_write receipt on the stale value: a *writer* , not a read, had landed an older version after pass 1. A long-running background job was exceeding its timeout but kept running, and the job queue redelivered it in the meantime. Several copies ended up updating the same rows at once, and whichever finished last could leave an outdated version in the cache. We fixed it by having the job stop well before its timeout and hand the remaining work to a fresh copy of itself, so a large job now runs as a chain of sequential tasks, one at a time.


### Impact


- **Every inconsistency comes with a cause.** The reconciler is no longer just a safety net; it tells us which part of the system broke consistency, per model, so on-call can tell a race from a bug at a glance.
- **Better observability into the cache.** Each receipt carries the writer’s service and trace ID, so a recent cache value can be traced to the request that wrote it, and the metric shows how each model’s cache is being filled.
- **Safer to extend.** Every cache write path must declare its operation, and the type checker enforces it. When a new model misses a cache write, it shows up under that model’s name.


### What we learned


- **Versioned rows make consistency decidable.** A monotonic db_version lets the writer, the cache, and the reconciler agree on what “stale” means.
- **Cache inconsistencies are often application bugs in disguise.** The cache is where they become visible.


*Thanks to*[Slava Markeyev](https://medium.com/@stlava) *,*[Ronak Shah](https://medium.com/@ronakts) *and Klaire Tan for their reviews and feedback. We kept the receipts.*
